newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban face coalition threat.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban face coalition threat.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban government faced the threat of strengthened links forged between its two most powerful adversaries on Tuesday, but the Islamic movement's leader still vowed to liberate areas outside its control.

One opponent, northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, has avoided committing his forces to either side in the country's latest conflict, but agreed on Monday to recognise deposed president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

The forces of Ahmad Shah Masood, Rabbani's former military chief, have consolidated gains north of the capital. It was not immediately possible to confirm their claims they had taken all but a corner of the important Bagram military airbase on Monday.
The capital itself was calm on Tuesday, with no signs of either a local uprising or the presence of Masood fighters in one district, as claimed by a Masood spokesman on Monday.
Taleban fighters briefly opened fire on Monday night but the firing appeared to be spontaneous and into the air.

The leader of the purist Islamic Taleban, who conquered Kabul on September 27 but have seen much of their lightning gains north of the capital rolled back in the past few days, appeared defiant and confident of taking northern territory held by the forces of Masood and Uzbek commander Dostum.

"I give you the good news that the sun of peace and tranquillity will soon shine, with the help of Almighty God, across the dark areas of the country," Mullah Amir Mohammad Omar, founder of the Taleban movement, said in a statement broadcast by Radio Afghanistan late on Monday.
But militarily and politically the situation did not augur well for the Taleban, who since their formation two years ago have swept into much of the country, Afghan-watchers said.

Their hopes of winning over Dostum, or persuading him to remain neutral, took another knock with Monday's agreement between the Uzbek leader, Tajik Masood and other leaders including Shi'ite Hazara Karim Khalili.
While much of the southern half of the country is made up of ethnic Pashtuns, the northern provinces are more fragmented, and have historically opposed Pashtun domination of the country.

Given the broad ethnic representation at the meeting and the military strength of Dostum and Masood combined, Taleban radicals' dreams of establishing an ultra-conservative Islamic hegemony over all of Afghanistan would seem to be over.

Dostum controls six provinces north of the Hindu Kush mountains, and his support is seen as vital for any push by Masood -- known for his guerrilla exploits against Soviet forces in the 1980s -- on Kabul.

Masood now holds the road and strategic towns of Jabal os-Siraj and Charikar on the plains between his base in the Panjsher Valley and Kabul. His gains leave him less than an hour's drive from the capital.

Kabul's fate remains uncertain. There was no decision about joint military operations by Dostum and Masood forces, but Dostum spokesman General Mohamed Youssef, speaking to reporters on Monday, did not rule out the possibility.
Taleban fighters were seen driving through the city in commandeered cars on Tuesday, a familiar sight, and the occasional tank rumbled by. Otherwise life was normal.
Journalists have been barred from leaving the city along its two northern roads since fighting worsened late last week.
